title: Physics Foundations: Set 3
description: Twelve original SL practice questions aligned with the current IB Physics syllabus, with checked answers and restrained diagrams.

questions.prompt: A sensor above a warm landscape detects infrared radiation travelling upward. Which process can return some of that energy toward the landscape? [1]
questions.hint: Consider what greenhouse-gas molecules do after absorbing outgoing infrared radiation.
notes: Greenhouse gases can absorb infrared photons emitted by a warm surface and later emit infrared radiation in different directions.
Radiation emitted toward the surface changes the outgoing energy balance. Absorption followed by emission is distinct from the surface simply reflecting sunlight.

options.label: A
options.text: The atmosphere absorbs mainly incoming visible light but transmits the outgoing infrared radiation.

options.label: B
options.text: Greenhouse-gas molecules absorb outgoing infrared radiation and emit some toward the surface.

options.label: C
options.text: Greenhouse-gas molecules emit the absorbed infrared radiation only upward into space.

options.label: D
options.text: The atmosphere returns outgoing infrared radiation solely by mirror-like reflection.

answer.explanation: B is correct: greenhouse gases absorb some outgoing infrared radiation and emit in different directions, including downward. A reverses the selective absorption, C omits downward emission and D mistakes molecular absorption/emission for mirror-like reflection.

questions.prompt: A spherical satellite of radius 2.0 m is illuminated by approximately parallel solar radiation of intensity 800 W m⁻². A detector measures 3.52 × 10³ W of solar power scattered by the satellite. Treat the scattering as contributing to its overall albedo, and ignore other incoming radiation.
questions.hint: Use the albedo to separate reflected and absorbed fractions. For a sphere, compare the intercepted disc area with the total surface area.

part_hints.label: a
part_hints.hint: First find the power intercepted by the projected circular area, then compare the measured scattered power with it.

part_hints.label: b
part_hints.hint: Use the complementary absorbed fraction and account for the sphere’s total area relative to its projected area.

part_hints.label: c
part_hints.hint: At equilibrium absorbed radiation balances thermal emission. Consider which surface property controls emission rate at a given temperature.

notes: Albedo is scattered power divided by incident power. For parallel illumination of a sphere, the intercepted power uses the projected area πr², not the total surface area.
The whole-sphere mean absorbed intensity is (1 − albedo)S/4. Estimating equilibrium temperature also needs a thermal-emission model, including emissivity and energy balance.

diagram.alt: Parallel rays illuminate a sphere of radius 2.0 m; the measured scattered solar power is 3.52 kW.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the albedo of the satellite. [2]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean solar intensity absorbed per unit area of its whole surface. [3]

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one additional surface property needed to estimate its equilibrium temperature and explain why. [2]

answer.explanation: Worked answers and one-mark criteria are given for each part.

marking_points.text: Uses incident power Sπr² for the projected disc.
Obtains albedo 0.350 (accept 0.35) from scattered/incident power.

parts.label: b
parts.working: Absorbed fraction = 1 − 0.35 = 0.65. Whole-sphere mean incident intensity = 800/4 = 200 W m⁻²; mean absorbed = 0.65 × 200 = 130 W m⁻².

marking_points.text: Uses absorbed fraction 1 − albedo = 0.65.
Accounts for projected πr² versus total 4πr² area, giving mean incident intensity S/4.
Obtains mean absorbed intensity 130 W m⁻²; follow-through from (a).

parts.label: c
parts.answer: Emissivity is needed because it sets thermal power emitted at a given temperature; equilibrium requires emitted and absorbed powers to balance.
parts.working: Thermal emission per unit area is εσT⁴. Without emissivity ε, the emitted power at each T cannot be calculated from the absorbed intensity alone.

marking_points.text: Identifies surface emissivity as a needed property.
Explains that emissivity controls emitted thermal intensity in the equilibrium energy balance.

questions.prompt: A sealed sample of ideal gas is first heated at constant volume until its absolute temperature doubles. It is then expanded isothermally to three times that volume. What is its final pressure as a fraction of its initial pressure? [1]
questions.hint: Track pressure after each stage using pV/T = constant for a fixed gas sample.
notes: For a fixed amount of ideal gas, pV/T is constant. At fixed volume pressure scales with absolute temperature.
At fixed temperature pressure is inversely proportional to volume. For successive stages, apply each ratio to the state produced by the previous stage.

answer.explanation: The first stage doubles the pressure. The second makes the volume three times greater at fixed temperature, so pfinal = 2pinitial/3.

questions.prompt: A rigid vessel of volume 0.100 m³ contains 2.00 × 10²² particles of an ideal gas at 300 K. Use kB = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹. The vessel remains sealed.
questions.hint: Use the particle form of the ideal-gas law. A sealed rigid vessel keeps both particle count and volume fixed.

part_hints.label: a
part_hints.hint: Rearrange pV = NkBT and keep the vessel volume in cubic metres.

part_hints.label: b
part_hints.hint: Think about molecular speeds, collisions with the wall and momentum transferred in those collisions.

part_hints.label: c
part_hints.hint: Use the absolute-temperature ratio because the vessel is sealed and rigid.

notes: The particle form pV = NkBT uses total particle number N, rather than amount in moles. Convert only if using pV = nRT.
At constant particle number and volume, pressure is proportional to absolute temperature. A temperature ratio must use kelvin.
At fixed particle number and volume, faster particles hit the walls more frequently and transfer more momentum per collision, increasing pressure.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gas pressure at 300 K. [2]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain, using the particle model, why heating the sealed rigid vessel increases its pressure. [3]

parts.label: c
parts.text: The gas warms to 450 K. Calculate its new pressure. [2]

answer.explanation: Worked answers and one-mark criteria are given for each part.

marking_points.text: Uses p = NkBT/V with the stated particle count, constant and volume.
Obtains 828 Pa.

parts.label: b
parts.answer: Greater absolute temperature raises mean molecular kinetic energy. Molecules move faster, collide with the walls more often, and transfer more momentum in each collision, raising pressure.
parts.working: At fixed N and V, heating increases mean translational kinetic energy and molecular speed. Wall collisions become more frequent and deliver greater impulse per collision, increasing mean force per area.

marking_points.text: Relates higher absolute temperature to greater mean molecular kinetic energy or speed.
Explains faster particles produce more frequent wall collisions in the fixed vessel.
Explains faster particles transfer more momentum per collision, increasing the rate of momentum transfer to the walls and therefore pressure.
Uses p₂/p₁ = T₂/T₁ for fixed N and V.
Obtains 1242 Pa (accept 1.24 × 10³ Pa); consistent follow-through from (a).

questions.prompt: A portable lamp receives 18 J of electrical energy as 3.0 C of charge passes through it. What is the potential difference across the lamp? [1]
questions.hint: Potential difference is transferred energy per unit charge.
notes: Potential difference is work or energy transferred per unit charge, V = W/q.
A joule per coulomb is one volt. Charge flow rate would require time and would instead determine current.

questions.prompt: A rechargeable cell has emf 9.0 V and internal resistance 1.5 Ω. It supplies a steady current of 2.0 A to one external resistor.
questions.hint: Treat the internal resistance as a series voltage drop. Useful external power uses the terminal potential difference.

part_hints.label: a
part_hints.hint: Find the voltage lost across the internal resistance, then subtract it from the emf.

part_hints.label: b
part_hints.hint: Use the current and terminal potential difference across the external resistor.

part_hints.label: c
part_hints.hint: Use emf for total cell power and I²r for the internal resistance.

notes: The terminal potential difference of a discharging cell is ε − Ir, where Ir is the internal voltage drop.
The power delivered to the external circuit is IVterminal. The cell also dissipates I²r internally, so emf × current is the total cell power.

diagram.alt: A cell with emf 9.0 V and internal resistance 1.5 ohms drives one external resistor at 2.0 A.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the terminal potential difference of the cell. [2]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the power delivered to the external resistor. [1]

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the total power supplied by the cell and the power dissipated in its internal resistance. Explain the difference from (b). [3]

answer.explanation: Worked answers and one-mark criteria are given for each part.

marking_points.text: Uses Vterminal = ε − Ir.
Obtains 6.0 V.
Obtains 12 W using current and terminal potential difference; follow-through from (a).

parts.label: c
parts.answer: 18 W total; 6.0 W dissipated internally as thermal energy, leaving 12 W externally.
parts.working: Pcell = Iε = 2.0 × 9.0 = 18 W. Pinternal = I²r = (2.0)²(1.5) = 6.0 W. The internal thermal dissipation accounts for the difference 18 − 12 = 6 W.

marking_points.text: Obtains total cell power Iε = 18 W.
Obtains internal dissipation I²r = 6.0 W.
Explains that internal heating accounts for the difference between total and external powers.

questions.prompt: An oscillator is displaced 0.040 m to the right of equilibrium and its acceleration is 1.6 m s⁻² to the left. When it is displaced 0.020 m to the left, which acceleration is consistent with simple harmonic motion? [1]
questions.hint: For simple harmonic motion, acceleration points toward equilibrium and its magnitude scales with displacement magnitude.
notes: Simple harmonic motion obeys a = −ω²x. The acceleration must have the opposite sign to displacement.
Halving the displacement magnitude halves the acceleration magnitude when ω is unchanged; the relation is linear.

answer.explanation: The new displacement has half the magnitude and opposite sign, so the acceleration is half as large and points right: 0.8 m s⁻².

questions.prompt: A 0.20 kg glider oscillates horizontally on a spring of spring constant 80 N m⁻¹. Friction is negligible. A second glider of mass 0.80 kg can be attached to the same spring instead.
questions.hint: Use the mass-spring period equation. Compare the two masses through their square roots, then convert period to frequency.

part_hints.label: a
part_hints.hint: Substitute mass in kilograms and spring constant in N m⁻¹ into T = 2π√(m/k).

part_hints.label: b
part_hints.hint: Compare masses under the square root before converting the new period to frequency.

part_hints.label: c
part_hints.hint: Inspect which quantities set T in the mass-spring relation.

notes: For a mass-spring oscillator, T = 2π√(m/k). At the same spring constant, period scales with √m.
Frequency is the reciprocal of period, f = 1/T. Increasing mass at fixed spring constant lowers frequency.
For ideal small-amplitude mass-spring SHM, T depends on mass and spring constant but not oscillation amplitude.

diagram.alt: Two gliders of masses 0.20 kg and 0.80 kg are considered separately on the same spring.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the period of the 0.20 kg glider. [2]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the period and frequency of the 0.80 kg glider on the same spring. [3]

parts.label: c
parts.text: State whether doubling the oscillation amplitude changes its period in the ideal simple-harmonic model. [1]

answer.explanation: Worked answers and one-mark criteria are given for each part.

marking_points.text: Uses T = 2π√(m/k) with the stated values.
Obtains 0.314 s (accept 0.31 s).
Uses the square-root mass scaling T₂/T₁ = 2 (or a direct valid mass-spring calculation).
Obtains the new period 0.628 s; follow-through from (a).
Obtains frequency 1.59 Hz from the reciprocal period; follow-through accepted.

parts.label: c
parts.working: T = 2π√(m/k), so the ideal model period is independent of amplitude.

marking_points.text: States the period remains unchanged when amplitude doubles within the ideal SHM model.

questions.prompt: A probe moves from just above the surface of a spherical moon of radius R to an altitude of 2R above that surface. What is the ratio of gravitational field strength at the new position to its surface value? [1]
questions.hint: Measure each distance from the moon centre, then use the inverse-square relation for field strength.
notes: Outside a spherical mass, g = GM/r², where r is centre-to-probe distance.
An altitude h above a body of radius R corresponds to r = R + h. Doubling altitude does not necessarily double r.

answer.explanation: The new centre distance is R + 2R = 3R, so gnew/gsurface = (R/3R)² = 1/9.

questions.prompt: A small spherical body has mass 4.0 × 10²³ kg and radius 2.0 × 10⁶ m. Assume it can be treated as a point mass when finding the field outside it. Use G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². A 2.0 kg test mass is used in part (b).
questions.hint: Use g = GM/r² with centre-to-point distance. Add radius and altitude before applying the inverse square.

part_hints.label: a
part_hints.hint: Use the body radius as the centre-to-point distance for the surface value.

part_hints.label: b
part_hints.hint: Add altitude to radius before finding field strength; force on a test mass follows F = mg.

notes: For a spherical body at an external point, gravitational field strength follows g = GM/r².
At altitude h, the distance r in the equation is R + h. A second point twice as far from the centre has one quarter the field strength.
Field strength is force per unit mass, so a test mass m at that point experiences gravitational force F = mg toward the field source.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gravitational field strength just above the surface. [2]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the field strength at an altitude of 2.0 × 10⁶ m and the force on a 2.0 kg test mass there. [3]

answer.explanation: Worked answers and one-mark criteria are given for each part.

marking_points.text: Uses g = GM/R² with the correct squared radius.
Obtains 6.67 N kg⁻¹ (accept 6.7 N kg⁻¹).

parts.label: b
parts.answer: 1.67 N kg⁻¹ and 3.34 N toward the body

marking_points.text: Uses centre distance r = R + h = 4.0 × 10⁶ m.
Obtains field strength 1.67 N kg⁻¹ by inverse-square scaling or GM/r²; follow-through from (a).
Obtains gravitational force 3.34 N toward the body using F = mg; follow-through accepted.

questions.prompt: A magnetic-field probe beside a long straight wire reads 6.0 μT north when the current is off. With a 2.0 A current in one direction, it reads 10.0 μT north. The current is reversed to 2.0 A without moving the probe. What does it now read? [1]
questions.hint: Find the wire’s field contribution from the two readings. Reversing the current reverses that contribution, while the background field stays the same.
notes: Magnetic fields at one point combine as vectors. Subtract a background reading to isolate the contribution of a current-carrying wire.
Reversing a straight-wire current reverses its magnetic-field direction at a fixed point while leaving its magnitude unchanged if the current magnitude is unchanged.

answer.explanation: The original wire contribution is 10.0 − 6.0 = 4.0 μT north. Reversing its current makes that 4.0 μT south. The unchanged background of 6.0 μT north leaves a resultant 2.0 μT north.

questions.prompt: Two large parallel plates are 0.015 m apart. Their potential difference is 450 V, and the field between them is approximately uniform. A small particle of charge +2.0 μC is placed between the plates. Ignore edge effects.
questions.hint: Use the plate potential difference and separation to find field strength. Then apply the force-per-charge definition.

part_hints.label: a
part_hints.hint: Divide the full potential difference by the full plate separation in metres.

part_hints.label: b
part_hints.hint: Use F = qE for magnitude; compare the positive charge with the field direction shown between the plates.

part_hints.label: c
part_hints.hint: At fixed potential difference, first consider how E = V/d changes.

notes: For a uniform field between parallel plates, E = V/d, with separation measured along the field.
Electric field strength is force per unit positive charge, so F = qE. A positive charge experiences force toward the negative plate.
At fixed plate potential difference, doubling separation halves uniform field strength and the force magnitude on an unchanged charge.

diagram.alt: Parallel positive and negative plates separated by 0.015 m with a positive test particle between them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the electric field strength between the plates. [2]

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the force magnitude and explain its direction using the sign of the particle’s charge. [3]

parts.label: c
parts.text: The plate separation is doubled while their potential difference stays 450 V. State how the force magnitude changes. [1]

answer.explanation: Worked answers and one-mark criteria are given for each part.

marking_points.text: Uses E = V/d with d = 0.015 m.
Obtains 3.0 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.working: F = (2.0 × 10⁻⁶)(3.0 × 10⁴) = 0.060 N. Electric field direction is from positive to negative plate; a positive charge experiences force along that direction.

marking_points.text: Uses F = qE with q = 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ C.
Obtains force magnitude 0.060 N; follow-through from (a).
Explains that a positive charge feels force with the field, toward the negative plate.

parts.label: c
parts.working: Doubling d halves E, so F = qE also halves.

marking_points.text: States that the force magnitude halves (to 0.030 N).
